n0001.title: Spider silk
n0001.gist: Spider silk's layered protein structure makes it remarkably strong and tough, inspiring artificial efforts to recreate it
n0001.question: Spider silk — why is it stronger and tougher than comparable materials, and can it be made artificially? (several lines of evidence)

n0002.title: Spider silk
n0002.gist: Spiders produce silk in many types to build webs, trap and wrap prey, protect offspring, and aid movement, courtship, and even feeding.
n0002.question: Spider silk — what is it and what roles does it serve in a spider's life? (an overview)

n0003.title: Title and credit
n0003.gist: The article's title and Wikimedia contributor credit.

n0006.title: Illustrations
n0006.gist: Two images show a spider wrapping prey in silk and a painting of gossamer thread, illustrating silk's long cultural presence.

n0009.title: What spider silk is
n0009.gist: Spiders spin silk for many purposes—trapping prey, signaling mates, suspending themselves, or ballooning through air—varying its thickness and stickiness, and sometimes even eating it as food.

n0013.title: Properties
n0013.gist: Spider silk's layered crystalline-and-amorphous protein structure gives it an unusual mix of strength, stretch, and adhesion that outperforms many engineered materials.
n0013.question: Properties — why does spider silk combine strength, toughness, and stickiness so effectively? (structural, mechanical, and adhesive evidence)

n0014.title: Structural
n0014.gist: Spider silk's proteins form a block copolymer whose stiff crystalline beta-sheets and stretchy amorphous regions combine to produce its unusual strength and elasticity, as models and imaging confirm.

n0022.title: Mechanical
n0022.gist: Dragline silk combines high tensile strength, elasticity, and low density to achieve exceptional toughness, with measured stiffness, strength, temperature tolerance, and water-triggered shrinkage surpassing many engineered fibres including Kevlar.

n0049.title: Adhesive
n0049.gist: Attachment-disc silk is a durable two-compound secretion that polymerises instantly at ambient conditions, acting like a biodegradable glue whose properties are controlled by the spinnerets.

n0052.title: Uses
n0052.gist: A single spider can spin up to seven silk types, each matched to a specific use such as catching prey, reproducing, or escaping danger.
n0052.question: Uses — how does silk's variety let spiders catch prey, reproduce, and move? (a list of uses)

n0053.title: Variety of silk uses
n0053.gist: Each spider can spin up to seven different silk types, unlike insects that make only one, reflecting silk's long evolutionary refinement from simple tube webs to complex orb webs.

n0056.title: Table of uses
n0056.gist: A table lists specific uses of silk, including prey capture, immobilisation, reproduction, dispersal, feeding, nest-building, guide lines, drop lines, alarm signals, and pheromone trails.

n0058.title: Silk types
n0058.gist: Different silk glands produce chemically distinct silks, each with properties suited to a particular structural or behavioral role in the web.
n0058.question: Silk types — how do a spider's different glands create silks suited to specific jobs? (a table of gland-silk-use pairings)

n0059.title: Overview and diagrams
n0059.gist: Diagrams identify seven distinct silk types—major and minor ampullate, flagelliform, piriform, tubuliform, aciniform, and aggregate—each suited to a different structural or defensive role.

n0064.title: Glands and silk types
n0064.gist: Each silk type is produced by a dedicated gland and matched to a specific job, from dragline strength to sticky capture threads to stiff protective egg-sac silk.

n0070.title: Synthesis and fibre spinning
n0070.gist: Silk fibre is pulled rather than extruded, formed inside a tapering duct where pH, water removal, and shear force convert liquid protein into solid fibre.
n0070.question: Spinning — how does a spider turn liquid silk protein into a solid fibre without external machinery? (a gland-by-gland account)

n0071.title: Spinning process
n0071.gist: Unlike continuously grown plant fibres, silk is pulled on demand from a liquid precursor stored in glands, a pulling process more akin to pultrusion than true spinning.

n0076.title: Silk gland
n0076.gist: The spinning duct tapers through sections—tail, ampulla, funnel, duct, and valve—where shear, acidification, and water removal convert liquid silk dope into an ordered solid fibre.

n0096.title: Artificial synthesis
n0096.gist: Replicating spider silk artificially requires both producing its unspun protein feedstock and mimicking the spinning geometry that turns it into fibre.
n0096.question: Artificial synthesis — why has it proven so hard to manufacture silk fibres that match natural spider silk? (several approaches compared)

n0097.title: Synthesis task
n0097.gist: Producing silk fibres artificially requires replicating both the liquid protein feedstock spiders make and the spinning conditions that convert it into solid fibre.

n0101.title: Feedstock
n0101.gist: Replicating silk's long, complex protein requires extracting or engineering suitable source organisms—spiders, silkworms, bacteria, goats, or plants—each yielding fibres with different strength and stretch.

n0105.title: Geometry
n0105.gist: Because artificial feedstock lacks a natural duct, researchers use needles, superhydrophobic surfaces, sheet self-assembly, microfluidics, or electrospinning to coax protein solutions into usable fibres.

n0119.title: Other shapes
n0119.gist: Beyond ordinary fibres, silk proteins can self-assemble into capsules, sheets, nanowires, and flexible membranes used for drug delivery, wound healing, and engineered tissue applications.

n0122.title: Synthetic spider silk
n0122.gist: Genetic engineering of bacteria, yeast, plants, and silkworms has produced spider silk-like proteins, spun by wet-spinning into fibres that remain weaker and simpler than natural dragline silk.

n0135.title: Research
n0135.gist: Decades of studies have progressively mapped spider silk's chemistry, structure, and mechanics, building the foundation for synthetic replication efforts.
n0135.question: Research — which studies established what we now know about spider silk's structure and properties? (a table of key papers)

n0138.title: Significant papers table
n0138.gist: A table lists landmark papers from 1960 to 2006 covering spider silk's chemical composition, gene sequence, mechanical properties, structure, and synthetic spinning, noting each study's key contribution.

n0140.title: Human uses
n0140.gist: Humans have long tried to harvest spider silk for textiles and now apply it in medicine, optics, and scientific instruments.
n0140.question: Human uses — how has spider silk moved from historical curiosity to modern scientific and medical application? (several applications)

n0141.title: Early silk fabric production
n0141.gist: Historical attempts to weave spider silk into cloth date to 1709, but harvesting silk at scale remains so difficult that only one large textile, made from a million spiders, has ever been produced.

n0146.title: Medicine
n0146.gist: Traditional Carpathian wound dressings used tube-web silk for its apparent antiseptic, vitamin-K-rich clotting properties, and modern research has tested spider silk for nerve regeneration.

n0149.title: Science and technology
n0149.gist: Spider silk's fineness and elasticity have suited it to optical crosshairs, diffraction experiments, biolenses, and even suspending fusion targets during laser ignition without introducing contaminating x-rays.
